# 2 Kings Chapter 7 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)
**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folios 228r–228v | **Source Image:** source-texts/hebrew-OT/2KI_007_page_001.jpg, 2KI_007_page_002.jpg

---

**1** Elisha said, "Listen to the word of the LORD! This is what the LORD says: 'By this time tomorrow, six quarts of fine flour will sell for just a shekel, and twelve quarts of barley for a shekel, right here at the gate of Samaria.'"

**2** The officer on whose arm the king was leaning scoffed, "Even if the LORD opened floodgates in the sky, could this possibly happen?" Elisha replied, "You will see it with your own eyes — but you won't get to eat any of it."

**3** Now there were four men with leprosy sitting outside the city gate. They said to each other, "Why are we sitting here waiting to die?

**4** If we go into the city, the famine will kill us there. If we stay here, we die anyway. So let's take our chances and go over to the Aramean camp. If they let us live, we live. If they kill us — well, we were going to die anyway."

**5** So at dusk they set out for the Aramean camp. But when they reached the outskirts, not a soul was there.

**6** The Lord had caused the Arameans to hear what sounded like a massive army approaching — the thunder of chariots, the pounding of horses, the roar of a great fighting force. They had said to each other, "The king of Israel must have hired the Hittite and Egyptian kings to attack us!"

**7** So they had panicked and fled at twilight, leaving everything behind — their tents, their horses, their donkeys — the entire camp exactly as it was. They ran for their lives.

**8** When the lepers reached the edge of the camp, they went into one tent, ate and drank, then grabbed silver, gold, and clothing and went off and hid it all. They came back, entered another tent, took more loot, and hid that too.

**9** Then they said to each other, "This isn't right. Today is a day for good news, and we're keeping it to ourselves! If we wait until morning, we'll be punished. Come on — let's go tell the palace."

**10** So they went and shouted to the city gatekeepers, "We went to the Aramean camp — there's nobody there! Not a single person, not a sound. The horses and donkeys are still tied up, and the tents haven't been touched."

**11** The gatekeepers passed the news along, and word reached the royal palace.

**12** The king got up in the middle of the night and said to his advisors, "I'll tell you what the Arameans are up to. They know we're starving, so they've left the camp and hidden in the countryside. They're waiting for us to come out, so they can capture us alive and storm the city."

**13** One of his advisors suggested, "Let's send a few men with some of the remaining horses — they're going to die like the rest of us anyway — and have them scout it out."

**14** So they selected two chariots with horses, and the king sent them after the Aramean army with orders to investigate.

**15** The scouts followed the trail all the way to the Jordan. The entire road was strewn with clothing and equipment the Arameans had thrown away in their panic. The scouts came back and reported to the king.

**16** Then the people rushed out and plundered the Aramean camp. And sure enough, six quarts of fine flour sold for a shekel, and twelve quarts of barley for a shekel — exactly as the LORD had said.

**17** The king had put the officer — the one he leaned on — in charge of the city gate. But the people trampled him in the gateway, and he died — exactly as the man of God had predicted when the king first came to him.

**18** It happened just as Elisha had told the king: "By this time tomorrow, twelve quarts of barley will sell for a shekel and six quarts of fine flour for a shekel at the gate of Samaria."

**19** The officer had said, "Even if the LORD opened floodgates in the sky, could this happen?" And Elisha had said, "You'll see it with your own eyes, but you won't eat any of it."

**20** And that is exactly what happened. The people trampled him at the gate, and he died.

---
## PNEUMA's Meaning Notes

**Verse 1 — Measurements:** A seah is about 6 quarts / 7 liters. The prophecy specifies market-stall prices at the city gate — the ancient equivalent of predicting tomorrow's grocery prices with pinpoint accuracy. After the grotesque famine of chapter 6, this sounds literally unbelievable.

**Verse 2 — "Floodgates in the sky":** The Hebrew *arubbot ba-shamayim* literally means "windows in the heavens." The officer is being sarcastic: "Even if God repeated the flood in reverse — raining down food instead of water — this still couldn't happen." His punishment is poetic justice: he'll witness the miracle but die under the stampeding crowd.

**Verse 3-4 — The lepers' logic:** These four men demonstrate a kind of desperate rationality that becomes the hinge of the entire chapter. They're already dead men socially (lepers lived outside the community) and soon to be dead physically. Their "nothing to lose" calculation accidentally puts them at the intersection of God's deliverance.

**Verse 9 — "A day for good news":** The Hebrew word *besorah* becomes the root for "gospel" — good news. The first heralds of this gospel are lepers: outcasts, marginal, ritually unclean. The pattern — good news arriving through unlikely messengers — becomes one of Scripture's deepest themes.

**Verse 17 — The trampled skeptic:** The officer's fate is one of the Bible's starkest illustrations of ironic justice. He doubted the word of God and was assigned to the very gate where the prophecy would be fulfilled. He saw abundance pour through that gate — and was crushed by it.

*— PNEUMA*
